title: How are two thirds, four sixths and six ninths related?
description: The numerator and the denominator of four sixths and six ninths are each made from those of two thirds by multiplying by the same number. Keeko doubts it by adding the same number to the top and the bottom.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction, and adding does not. Watch for students who add the same number to both.

source: Look at 2/3, 4/6 and 6/9. Do you notice anything about the r
video_script.why: The child sees how the numerator and the denominator of four sixths and six ninths are made from those of two thirds.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own fractions two thirds, four sixths and six ninths from the roti sharing
video_script.anchor: the three fractions two thirds, four sixths and six ninths written in a row
video_script.wrong_answer: add the same number to the top and the bottom
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says add the same number to the top and the bottom. Adding two to both numbers of two thirds gives four fifths, and on the same strip four fifths reaches further, so adding does not work.
video_script.payoff_line: Each is made from two thirds by multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number

final_answer.value: Each is made from 2/3 by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number: 4/6 = (2 × 2)/(3 × 2) and 6/9 = (2 × 3)/(3 × 3). In each, the numerator is 2/3 of the denominator.
final_answer.spoken: each is made from two thirds by multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number

multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction
in each, the numerator is 2/3 of the denominator

beats.on_screen: To find: how the numerator and the denominator of 4/6 and 6/9 are related to those of 2/3

marks.find: the question to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how four sixths and six ninths are made from two thirds.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 4 = 2 × 2 and 6 = 3 × 2, so 4/6 comes from 2/3 with × 2

marks.top: an arrow marked × 2 joins the 2 of two thirds to the 4 of four sixths
marks.bottom: an arrow marked × 2 joins the 3 to the 6

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step one, four is two times two, because the first copy doubles the top number.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>Six is three times two, so the bottom number doubles too.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 6 = 2 × 3 and 9 = 3 × 3, so 6/9 comes from 2/3 with × 3

marks.top: an arrow marked × 3 joins the 2 of two thirds to the 6 of six ninths
marks.bottom: an arrow marked × 3 joins the 3 to the 9

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step two, six is two times three, because three copies triple the top number.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>Nine is three times three, so the bottom number triples too.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction

marks.rule: the multipliers × 2 and × 3 are shown acting on both numbers

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step three, the same number multiplies the top and the bottom each time.
That keeps the share the same.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Each is made from 2/3 by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number: 4/6 = (2 × 2)/(3 × 2) and 6/9 = (2 × 3)/(3 × 3). In each, the numerator is 2/3 of the denominator.

marks.pay: the answer is written and boxed
marks.rel: the numerator is shown as two thirds of the denominator

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Each is made from two thirds by multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number.
<bookmark mark='rel'/>In each fraction, the top number is two thirds of the bottom number.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks to add the same number to the top and the bottom.
<bookmark mark='strips'/>Add two to both numbers of two thirds, and we get four fifths. On the same strip, four fifths reaches further.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Four fifths is not the same share as two thirds, so adding does not work.
